sections.title: Meeting the Human-Machine Interface
learningObjectives: Understand what the ANT interface is, and that you do not need a technical background to use it
Recognize the difference between monitoring MoRo and actively controlling it
sections.content: Every MoRo unit is managed through a Human-Machine Interface (HMI) — software that lets an operator see and direct what the machine is doing, rather than controlling it through physical switches alone. MoRo's HMI is called ANT. You don't need a technical background to use it. Most day-to-day interaction is supervisory: you observe operations, confirm actions, and intervene only when needed — not continuous hands-on control.

keyTerms.note: The software layer through which an operator interacts with and monitors a machine's operations.
MoRo's HMI platform, used for fleet monitoring and mission control.
Overseeing an automated system's operation without directly performing each action yourself.

video.title: Meet the control interface in 30 seconds
video.transcript: The control interface, in 30 seconds. MoRo is managed through software: the HMI. On MoRo, it is called ANT. You do not need a technical background. Most of the time, you supervise. You observe and confirm actions. You step in only when needed.

sections.title: Reading the Dashboard
learningObjectives: Identify the main categories of information on the dashboard
Know where to find MoRo's current status versus its assigned tasks
sections.content: The ANT dashboard answers three things: where MoRo is and what state it is in (fleet status), what it is assigned to do right now (mission status), and what the configuration options are (system settings). The exact menu structure and terminology within ANT will be confirmed against the live system before this section is finalized — the operational logic described here holds regardless of the final interface layout.

keyTerms.note: A real-time view of where each MoRo unit is and what state it's in.
The current and queued tasks assigned to a unit.

sections.title: Startup Sequence
learningObjectives: List the startup sequence: visual check, power on, wait for the ready state, then assign a mission
Understand why the ready state matters before assigning work
sections.content: Startup follows a defined sequence, not a single action. Before power-on, conduct a visual check to confirm the intended path is clear and sensors are unobstructed. On power-on, MoRo runs an internal diagnostic — verifying battery charge, navigation calibration, and safety system function — before reporting a ready state. Operators must wait until MoRo reports the ready state before assigning a mission; assigning work before diagnostics complete is a common, avoidable cause of interrupted starts.

keyTerms.note: MoRo's automatic self-check of its systems (battery, navigation, safety) run at startup.
The confirmed status indicating MoRo has passed its startup diagnostic and can accept mission assignments.

video.title: The startup sequence in 30 seconds
video.transcript: The startup sequence, in 30 seconds. First, a visual check: path clear, sensors unobstructed. Then power on: MoRo runs its own diagnostic. It checks battery, navigation and safety systems. Wait for the ready state. Only then assign a mission. Assigning early: a common cause of interrupted starts.

sections.title: Manual Override & Emergency Stop
learningObjectives: Understand when manual override is appropriate versus autonomous operation
Know how emergency stop functions relative to manual and autonomous modes
sections.content: MoRo operates autonomously by default. Manual override exists for specific situations — repositioning during setup, clearing a blocked path, or post-maintenance testing. Manual override does not disable safety systems. Emergency stop (E-stop) functions identically in both manual and autonomous modes: it takes immediate priority and halts all operation regardless of current state.

keyTerms.note: Operator-initiated direct control of MoRo, used for specific non-routine situations.
MoRo's default operating state, in which it executes missions independently.
An immediate, unconditional halt command that overrides all other operation.

video.title: Manual override and E-stop in 30 seconds
video.transcript: Manual override and E-stop, in 30 seconds. MoRo works autonomously by default. Override: setup repositioning, a blocked path, post-maintenance tests. Manual override does not disable safety systems. E-stop works the same in both modes. It takes immediate priority and halts all operation.

sections.title: Mission Lifecycle
learningObjectives: Describe the basic mission lifecycle: load, start, monitor, pause, resume
Understand what happens to a paused mission
sections.content: A mission moves through a defined lifecycle: it's loaded, started, monitored during execution, and can be paused or resumed as needed. Pausing a mission is not the same as cancelling it — MoRo holds position safely and resumes from the same point once cleared. Understanding this lifecycle is the operational foundation for everything covered in L2.

sections.title: Status Indicators
learningObjectives: Recognize what MoRo's status indicators communicate at a glance
Know the three general kinds of status signal: normal operation, waiting or paused, and attention-needed
sections.content: Beyond the dashboard, MoRo communicates status directly through visual indicators — useful for floor-level awareness without checking a screen. These fall into general categories: normal operation, waiting/paused, and attention-needed. The confirmed color-and-pattern reference will be added once verified against current MoRo hardware documentation.

keyTerms.note: A visual signal (light) on the MoRo unit itself that communicates its current operating state.

questions.question: How will you usually work with MoRo through ANT?
options: Steer it by hand the whole time
Watch operations, confirm actions, and step in only when needed
Use it only after something goes wrong
questions.feedback: Correct. Most day-to-day interaction is supervisory: you observe operations, confirm actions, and intervene only when needed.

questions.question: Which order is correct for starting MoRo?
options: Power on, assign a mission, then do the visual check
Power on, do the visual check, then assign a mission while the diagnostic runs
Visual check, power on, wait for the ready state, then assign a mission
questions.feedback: Correct. Check the path and sensors first, power on, wait for the ready state, and only then assign a mission. Assigning before diagnostics complete is a common, avoidable cause of interrupted starts.

questions.question: MoRo is in manual override and someone triggers the E-stop. What happens?
options: MoRo finishes its current move, then stops
All operation halts immediately, the same as in autonomous mode
Nothing, because E-stop works only in autonomous mode
questions.feedback: Correct. E-stop works the same in manual and autonomous modes: it takes immediate priority and halts all operation regardless of current state.

questions.question: A mission is paused, not cancelled. What happens?
options: MoRo holds position safely and resumes from the same point once cleared
It starts again from the beginning
MoRo returns to its charging dock automatically
questions.feedback: Correct. Pausing a mission is not the same as cancelling it: MoRo holds position safely and resumes from the same point once cleared.

questions.question: You are on the floor with no screen nearby. How can you tell at a glance what state a MoRo is in?
options: The status indicator on the unit
questions.feedback: Correct. Status indicators on the unit show its operating state at a glance, useful for floor-level awareness without checking a screen.
